summary: Defines MIB objects for remote network monitoring (RMON) on high-speed networks, along with updated objects from the RMON-MIB. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Watching traffic on fast networks needs counters that do not overflow. This adds bigger counters.

questions: what is rmon high capacity mib
what is a counter64 in snmp
how does rmon handle counter overflow
subtitle: SNMP objects for RMON probes that add 64-bit and overflow counters so monitoring keeps up with fast networks.

tldr.problem: The RMON statistics counters of the original RMON and RMON-2 MIBs are 32 bits wide, which are not enough for the traffic volumes of high speed networks.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3273 defines the HC-RMON-MIB, a set of tables that sit alongside the existing RMON tables and add overflow counters and 64-bit counters. It also adds a media independent statistics table and extends three TopN rate-base enumerations.
tldr.outcome: A probe implements the groups it needs as units of conformance. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 4502.

today: RFC 3273 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2002 and has been updated by RFC 4502. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: RMON for High Speed Networks
sections.content:
RFC 3273 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing remote network monitoring (RMON) devices on high speed networks. It continues the architecture of the RMON MIB in RFC 2819 and also contains updated objects from the RMON-2 MIB in RFC 2021.

Remote monitoring devices, often called monitors or probes, exist only to help manage a network. They are often stand-alone instruments with significant resources, perhaps one per network segment, or used by a management service provider to reach a remote client network.

The objects are meant as an interface between an RMON agent and an RMON management application, not for people to handle directly. Few users will tolerate manually creating rows, so the RFC says those functions should be handled by the management application.
sections.eli5: A probe is like a person counting cars on a road. This document gives the counting person a bigger notebook so they do not run out of numbers when the road gets very busy.

sections.title: The SNMP Management Framework
sections.content:
The memo opens by describing the SNMP Management Framework in five components: an architecture, the Structure of Management Information (SMI) for describing and naming objects, message protocols for transferring management information, protocol operations for accessing it, and a set of fundamental applications together with view-based access control.

Managed objects are reached through a virtual information store, the Management Information Base (MIB), and are defined with the SMI. This memo is written in SMIv2. A MIB in SMIv1 form can be produced by translation, which should be semantically equivalent except where an object cannot be translated, namely those using Counter64.

That caveat matters here, because the 64-bit counters are exactly the objects an SMIv1 translation cannot carry.
sections.eli5: SNMP is a way for a manager program to ask machines questions about themselves. The MIB is the list of all the questions that can be asked.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB and Its Groups
sections.content:
Except for mediaIndependentTable, every table in this MIB adds high capacity capability to an associated table in the RMON-1 or RMON-2 MIB. The objects are arranged into groups: mediaIndependentGroup, etherStatsHighCapacityGroup, etherHistoryHighCapacityGroup, hostHighCapacityGroup, hostTopNHighCapacityGroup, matrixHighCapacityGroup, captureBufferHighCapacityGroup, protocolDistributionHighCapacityGroup, the network layer groups (nlHost, nlMatrix, nlMatrixTopN), the application layer groups (alHost, alMatrix, alMatrixTopN) and usrHistoryHighCapacityGroup.

These groups are the basic units of conformance. If a monitoring device implements a group, it must implement every object in that group. For example, an agent that implements the network layer matrix group must implement both nlMatrixSDHighCapacityTable and nlMatrixDSHighCapacityTable. Implementations must also implement the system and interfaces groups of MIB-II.
sections.eli5: The new counters are sorted into labeled boxes. If a probe takes one box, it must take everything inside it, not just a few items.

sections.title: High Capacity Counters and the Media Independent Table
sections.content:
The core idea is a three-part pattern repeated across tables. An existing 32-bit counter such as etherStatsPkts can wrap around. For it, the HC-RMON-MIB adds an overflow counter (a Counter32 that records the number of times the associated counter has overflowed) and a high capacity counter (a Counter64 holding the full total). For example, etherStatsHighCapacityOverflowPkts and etherStatsHighCapacityPkts extend etherStatsTable. The same pattern covers octet counts, the packet-size buckets such as 64 octets and 1024 to 1518 octets, host tables, conversation matrices, protocol distribution and user history.

The one genuinely new table is mediaIndependentTable. It provides statistics for promiscuous monitoring of any media, including full and half-duplex links. For half-duplex links the mediaIndependentIn* objects are used and the mediaIndependentOut* objects do not increment. For full-duplex links the Out objects are present and increment. Each entry is indexed by mediaIndependentIndex (1 to 65535), names its source interface through mediaIndependentDataSource, and reports drop events, dropped frames, packets, octets, non-unicast packets, errors, nominal speed in kilobits per second, duplex mode (halfduplex(1) or fullduplex(2)) and duplex changes.

The RFC also adds a time stamp refinement. captureBufferPacketHighCapacityTime returns nanoseconds, modulo 10^6, to add to the millisecond value in captureBufferPacketTime, giving a more accurate inter-packet arrival time.

Utilization on half-duplex Fast Ethernet can be estimated from etherStatsHighCapacityOctets and the packet count sampled before and after an interval. For full-duplex ethernet, the RFC says to compute inbound and outbound utilization separately using the media independent table and take the maximum.
sections.eli5: A small odometer rolls back to zero after 99999 miles. This design keeps a tally of how many times it rolled over and also adds a giant odometer that almost never fills up.

sections.title: Updates to RMON and RMON-2 Objects
sections.content:
The RFC extends the enumerations of three existing objects so that TopN reports can be sorted on high capacity values and written to high capacity tables. In each case, the value chosen both selects the variable to rank by and controls which table receives the report.

For hostTopNRateBase in the RMON MIB, new values 8 to 11 (hostTopNHCInPkts, hostTopNHCOutPkts, hostTopNHCInOctets, hostTopNHCOutOctets) send results to hostTopNHighCapacityTable, while values 7 or less still use hostTopNTable. nlMatrixTopNControlRateBase in RMON-2 gains values 3 and 4, which use nlMatrixTopNHighCapacityTable. alMatrixTopNControlRateBase gains values 5 to 8 for high capacity packets and octets, in both terminal-only and all-protocols views.

These objects may not be modified while the associated status object is valid or active.
sections.eli5: When you ask for a top-ten list, you also pick which size of counter to rank by. Picking a big counter puts the list in the big-counter notebook.

sections.title: Compliance and Capabilities
sections.content:
The module ends with compliance statements and object groups. The media independent compliance requires mediaIndependentGroup and hcRMONInformationGroup. Others cover RMON-1 and RMON-2 high capacity support. Most high capacity groups are optional but require implementation of the corresponding base group. For instance, etherStatsHighCapacityGroup requires rmonEtherStatsGroup. The hostHighCapacityGroup is mandatory when hostTopNHighCapacityGroup is implemented.

A probe can report what it supports through hcRMONCapabilities, a bit string with one bit per group, from mediaIndependentGroup(0) to usrHistoryHighCapacityGroup(14). It indicates the groups supported on at least one interface of the probe.

The RFC also defines good packets (error-free and a valid frame length, on Ethernet between 64 and 1518 octets) and bad packets (properly framed but containing errors or an invalid length).
sections.eli5: A probe can fill in a checklist saying which of the big-counter features it has, so a manager knows what to ask for.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
To implement this MIB, a probe must capture all packets on its local network, including packets between third parties, and analyze them to collect addresses, protocol usage and conversation statistics. The RFC notes this data may be sensitive in some environments, so administrators may wish to restrict SNMP access to the probe. A probe is likely to also implement RMON, which can return the contents of captured packets, possibly including passwords, so SNMP access to those functions should be restricted.

Objects with read-write or read-create access can be sensitive, and SET support without proper protection can hurt network operations. SNMPv1 on its own is not secure, even on a network secured by IPsec. Implementers are urged to consider SNMPv3, specifically the User-based Security Model and the View-based Access Control Model, and operators must configure the SNMP entity so only legitimate principals can read or change the objects.
sections.eli5: A probe sees everything that passes by, even private stuff. So only trusted people should be allowed to ask it questions.

items.title: Existing counter
items.text: The 32-bit counter from the original RMON table, which can wrap around.

items.title: Overflow counter
items.text: A Counter32 that counts how many times the existing counter has overflowed.

items.title: High capacity counter
items.text: A Counter64 holding the full total of packets or octets.
